sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Describes Part Two as 'a summary of phonology, noun classes and pronominal forms for each of the six languages. The phonology has very modest claims'; no prosodic detail.

sources.citation: Seligmann, Brenda Z. 1911. Note on the language of the Nubas of Southern Kordofan. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 1: 167-188.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Only a transcription note, p.171: 'Long and short vowels are marked.. and stress is indicated by ´'. Eliri (=Nding, village Dayo) words in the comparative tables carry occasional acute marks; no statement of where stress falls. This is the sole primary data behind Meinhof's 1916-17 sketch.

sources.citation: Quint, Nicolas. 2020. Kordofanian. In R. Vossen & G. Dimmendaal (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of African Languages. Oxford: OUP (HAL halshs-03093501).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nding listed among nine Talodian languages; one lexical item cited; family-level 'probably all Kordofanian languages are tone languages'; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Smits, Heleen. 2017. A Grammar of Lumun, a Kordofanian language of Sudan. Vol. 1 (LOT 465). Utrecht: LOT.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nding mentioned only in the classification of Talodi; nothing on Nding prosody.

sources.citation: Norton, Russell & Thomas Kuku Alaki. 2015. The Talodi languages: a comparative-historical analysis. Occasional Papers in the Study of Sudanese Languages 11: 47-161.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: a catalogue record only (no print holding to request from, no digital copy known)
sources.note: Nding entry p.56 (data taken entirely from Schadeberg 1981; no fresh data). Sec. 3.2.5 'Note on Length and Tone' p.107: 'We omit analysis of prosodic features for lack of data and for lack of functional load.. Sources repeatedly show two tone levels in Talodi languages.. but tone is often contextually determined and minimal pairs are rare.' Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Tucker, A. N. & M. A. Bryan. 1966. Linguistic Analyses: The Non-Bantu Languages of North-Eastern Africa. London: OUP/IAI. ch. 18a (Koalib-Moro, Talodi-Masakin, Lafofa), sec. 2b Stress.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library, call number 2235.4.26; Linguistics Library, call number CoPh 36.88)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library, call number 2235.4.26; Linguistics Library, call number CoPh 36.88
sources.note: Group-level, second-hand from Stevenson 1956-57: "According to Stevenson 'dynamic Stress, accompanied by High or Low tone, plays a greater role than syllabic pitch as such, but is not equally prominent in all languages'. Examples are not marked for tone or stress." No placement rule; nothing Eliri-specific (snippet reconstruction by a sibling check; book is lending-only on archive.org).

sources.citation: Schadeberg, Thilo C. 1981. A Survey of Kordofanian. Vol. 2: The Talodi Group (Sprache und Geschichte in Afrika, Beiheft 2). Hamburg: Helmut Buske. 175 pp. -- Nding (Liri) chapter, '2.1 Phonological notes' (c. 3 pp.) + tone-marked 200-word data sheet.

sources.note: The only modern first-hand phonological notes on Nding (fieldwork 1974-75); chapter-final remarks on vowel length/tone are where any accent statement would be; only snippets readable (GB yYcOAAAAYAAJ).
